summary: A best current practice that says specifications of protocols using transient numeric identifiers must consider the security and privacy consequences of how they are generated. Poor choices have caused attacks like denial of service, data injection, and information leaks.

eli5.summary: If ticket numbers are easy to guess, bad guys can sneak in. Protocol makers should choose them carefully.

questions: security considerations for transient numeric identifiers
why predictable tcp sequence numbers are bad
what is a transient numeric identifier
why are predictable tcp sequence numbers bad

subtitle: Why protocol designers must think about how identifiers like sequence numbers and ports get chosen, not just that they are unique.

tldr.problem: Poorly chosen transient numeric identifiers, such as TCP sequence numbers, IPv6 interface identifiers and DNS IDs, have enabled denial of service, data injection and information leaks for over 30 years.
tldr.mechanism: Specifications that use such identifiers MUST state their interoperability requirements, MUST include a vulnerability assessment, SHOULD avoid predictable values and SHOULD recommend a generation algorithm that mitigates the findings.
tldr.outcome: The RFC formally updates RFC 3552 so that these identifiers are covered in the Security Considerations of future RFCs.

today: RFC 9416 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 72) that updates RFC 3552, and per the metadata it has not been obsoleted or updated itself.

sections.title: The Problem with Predictable Identifiers
sections.content:
Protocols use many transient numeric identifiers: IPv4 and IPv6 Identification values, IPv6 Interface Identifiers (IIDs), ephemeral port numbers, TCP Initial Sequence Numbers (ISNs), NTP Reference IDs and DNS IDs. Each has its own requirements, such as uniqueness for a period of time.

For more than 30 years, implementations have been attacked through poor selection of these values, with effects from denial of service and data injection to information leaks usable for pervasive monitoring. The root cause has often been insufficient or misleading specifications. The RFC lists predictable IP Identification values, IPv6 IIDs, ephemeral ports, TCP ISNs, initial TCP timestamps and DNS IDs as examples.

Cryptography does not make the problem go away. Authentication can stop data injection even with predictable sequence numbers, but flawed algorithms such as global counters can still leak information that enables other attacks. Related background is in RFC 9414 and RFC 9415.
sections.eli5: If a locker combination is just the next number after the last person's, anyone can guess it. Computers have the same problem with some of their numbers, and locks alone do not always fix it.

sections.title: Key Terms
sections.content:
A transient numeric identifier is a data object in a protocol specification that can definitely distinguish a protocol object (a datagram, network interface, transport endpoint, session and so on) from others of the same type in a given context. It is usually a series of bits shown as an integer and is dynamically selected, unlike statically assigned identifiers.

Failure severity describes the consequences of not meeting an identifier's requirements. A soft failure is recoverable automatically in a short time, such as a packet loss recovered by retransmission. A hard failure is non-recoverable or causes excessive degradation, such as an established TCP connection aborted by an error.
sections.eli5: A transient identifier is a name tag handed out just for now. A soft failure is a small hiccup that fixes itself. A hard failure is when things break for good.

sections.title: How Specifications Go Wrong
sections.content:
Most issues come from one of three conditions: specifications that under specify an identifier, specifications that over specify it, or implementations that fail to follow the specification.

TCP local ports and DNS IDs were originally under specified, so implementations produced predictable values vulnerable to off-path attacks. IPv6 IIDs and IPv6 Identification values were over specified, which left implementations unable to respond to security and privacy problems with the mandated or recommended algorithms. Some popular operating systems still fail to implement the port randomization specified in RFC 6056.

Clearly stating interoperability requirements helps identify suitable algorithms and shows when an identifier is over specified. A vulnerability assessment helps stop security considerations being overlooked.
sections.eli5: If the rules say nothing, people pick lazy, guessable numbers. If the rules force one bad method, nobody can switch to a better one. And some people just ignore the rules.

sections.title: Common Flaws in Generating Identifiers
sections.content:
The RFC lists flaws that are common but not exhaustive: trivial algorithms such as global counters, the same identifier across contexts that do not need constancy, reuse across protocols or layers, constant initial values for counters or timers, a shared increment space across contexts, and flawed Pseudorandom Number Generators (PRNGs).

Trivial algorithms let any node that samples identifiers predict future ones. Constant identifiers across networks allow tracking and activity correlation. Reusing an identifier across layers ties one protocol's security and privacy to another's and makes assessment harder. A shared increment space lets an attacker sampling one context learn how many identifiers were generated between two sampled values.
sections.eli5: Handing out tickets 1, 2, 3 lets anyone guess the next one. Using the same secret code everywhere lets someone follow you around. Using a broken dice for random numbers is just as bad.

sections.title: Requirements for Protocol Designers
sections.content:
Specifications that employ transient numeric identifiers:

  • MUST explicitly specify interoperability requirements, such as uniqueness, along with the failure severity if they are not met.
  • MUST include a vulnerability assessment as part of the specification process, covering at least spoofing, tampering, repudiation, information disclosure, DoS and elevation of privilege.
  • SHOULD NOT employ predictable identifiers, except when predictability results from interoperability requirements.
  • SHOULD recommend an algorithm that mitigates the vulnerabilities found, such as those discussed in RFC 9415.

This advice MUST still be applied when cryptography for confidentiality or authentication is used.
sections.eli5: When you invent a new numbering system, say what the numbers are for, think about how a bad guy could abuse them, and pick a hard-to-guess method.

sections.title: Security and IANA Considerations
sections.content: The whole document is about the security and privacy implications of transient numeric identifiers. It formally updates RFC 3552 so that these implications are addressed when writing the Security Considerations section of future RFCs. It has no IANA actions.
sections.eli5: This document adds one more question to the safety checklist that every new protocol document must answer.

items.title: Trivial algorithms
items.text: Global counters make future identifiers predictable.

items.text: Constancy across networks allows node tracking.

items.text: Ties one protocol's security and privacy to another's.

items.title: Constant initial values
items.text: Counters or timers start at fixed values without need.

items.title: Shared increment space
items.text: Reveals how many identifiers were generated between samples.

items.title: Flawed PRNGs
items.text: Weak random number generators produce guessable values.
